primary_claim: Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latent activations as a hypothesis space for text-data analysis outperforms an LLM-pipeline baseline at data diffing (e.g. discovering that Grok-4 is uniquely careful to clarify ambiguities among frontier models) and at recovering injected dataset correlations (down to a 10-in-10,000 base rate, more reliably than an LLM-judge baseline), while enabling property-based text clustering and retrieval that is on par with or exceeds state-of-the-art embedding methods without any finetuning

effect.metric: average verified hypothesis difference frequency (data diffing); correlation-recovery reliability; retrieval MAP/P@50 vs. embedding baselines
effect.value: SAE data-diffing average verified difference 7.03% (LLaVA-Next vs. Vicuna-7B) and 26-47% for frontier models, vs. a weaker LLM baseline; SAE correlation method recovers injected correlations down to a 10/10,000 base rate, more reliably than an LLM-judge baseline; SAE retrieval on par with or exceeding state-of-the-art embedding methods with no finetuning

contradicts_or_qualifies: conflicting evidence on SAE utility (Subhash et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.16681); this work provides positive evidence for SAE usefulness specifically for data-centric analysis tasks rather than model-internals interpretability
stated_future_work: obtain more accurate labels for all SAE latents to improve results
explore whether different SAEs are better suited depending on the analysis question, since SAE features depend on training data
study longer texts (e.g. agent transcripts), which would likely surface more complex, interesting insights
develop data-centric interpretability further as a promising general research direction
limitations_stated: work is a proof of concept; many areas for potential improvement remain
SAE latent labels are often noisy, overly specific, or duplicated (e.g. 537 different latents all labelled 'Offensive request from the user')
targeted clustering failed to recover ground-truth labels for sentiment and emotion classification tasks
retrieval performance is sensitive to the temperature used to aggregate latents; low temperatures perform poorly due to label noisiness
only studied relatively short pieces of text (below 2048 tokens due to API context limits)
quote: The average difference of our hypotheses is 7.03% for LLaVA-Next v. Vicuna-7B and ranges from 26-47% for the frontier models, suggesting that SAEs can identify strong differences.
